paper_title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) jointly process images, videos, audio, and text, supporting multimodal understanding and reasoning (Bai et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b; Google, 2025). Recent MLLMs can revisit relevant temporal clips (Yang et al., 2026a; Zeng et al., 2026b), inspect task-relevant spatial evidence (Wang et al., 2026c; Meng et al., 2026), and selectively acquire audio-visual evidence during reasoning (Xing et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). These advances motivate evaluating omni-modal video grounding and understanding. This requires identifying targets from textual or visual cues, grounding them spatiotemporally, and integrating audio-visual evidence to understand events. With the rapid development of MLLMs, how to comprehensively evaluate their performance in complex video understanding tasks has become an important problem. Table 1 compares existing benchmarks across four dimensions. (i) Target Specification defines how targets are presented: through only textual queries (Fu et al., 2025a) or with reference images (Ma et al., 2026). (ii) Video Evidence distinguishes tasks resolved from video frames (Chen et al., 2025a) from those requiring synchronized audio-visual content (Hong et al., 2026). (iii) Task Coverage specifies the output: temporal grounding (TG) and spatial grounding (SG) predict target-specific intervals and regions (Lei et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2026), while question answering (QA) predicts answers (Fu et al., 2026). (iv) Video Duration determines the temporal scope: short-video benchmarks emphasize fine-grained motion and local dynamics (Li et al., 2024b), whereas long-video benchmarks test long-range dependencies and information integration across temporally distant events (Zhou et al., 2025a). Despite this progress, existing benchmarks have three limitations in systematically diagnosing omni-modal video grounding and understanding. (i) Limited video-evidence coverage. Benchmarks typically assess either visual information (Chen et al., 2025a) or synchronized audio-visual content (Hong et al., 2026). In news broadcasts, some queries concern visible scenes; others require aligning spoken reports with people or events. Both settings are needed to assess visual perception and audio-visual integration. (ii) Inflexible target-specification settings. Most benchmarks use only text (Fu et al., 2026), while IV-Bench combines Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 2 / Figure 2. Overview of OmniCompass. The benchmark spans four dimensions: target specification, video evidence, task coverage, and video duration. Paired Text/Text+Image specifications are evaluated on the same targets. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances, while the 240-video OmniCompass-AV subset contains 720 instances with native audio. Both tracks cover temporal grounding, spatial grounding, and question answering. reference images with text (Ma et al., 2026). Practical targets may be specified verbally or with an image, yet these benchmarks do not evaluate the same target under both settings. (iii) Fragmented task coverage. Most benchmarks focus on QA (Li et al., 2024b) or grounding (Gao et al., 2026); audio-visual benchmarks rarely cover the latter (Li et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025b). In basketball games, users may ask when referenced player scores, where the player is on the court, and what happens. Joint evaluation distinguishes failures in temporal retrieval, spatial localization, and semantic understanding. To address these gaps, we introduce OmniCompass, holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding (i) Complementary and understanding. As shown in Figure 2, OmniCompass has four key features: Video Evidence. OmniCompass-VL evaluates understanding from visual content, while OmniCompass-AV additionally requires audio. (ii) Flexible Target Specification. Each instance pairs Text and Text+Image settings, specifying the same target through language alone or with reference image. The video, task semantics, and ground truth are the same. We introduce Cross-Specification Consistency Scores (CS) to jointly measure task accuracy and prediction consistency across these settings. (iii) Unified Task Coverage. Both tracks provide TG, SG, and QA tasks per video. The VL track covers five perception and three reasoning categories, whereas the AV track covers three perception and two reasoning categories. (iv) Diverse Durations and Content. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across short, medium, and long durations. It combines public sports, traffic, surveillance, and documentary videos with 240 self-collected movie, TV, variety, and news videos. This subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 720 instances. We evaluate 50 MLLMs, including proprietary and open-source models. The best proprietary model exceeds the best open-source model by 3.2% in CSAvg on VL track and 32.8% on AV track. Strong QA performance coexists with weak grounding and cross-reference inconsistency, even when aggregate accuracies are similar across settings. Visual target specifications do not consistently help: Text+Image improves the single-setting average for only 11 of 36 models. Further analyses show that timestamps substantially improve model performance across tasks and tracks, while audio consistently improves QA and TG performance on AV track. Future MLLMs therefore need stronger cross-modal alignment and more reliable audio-aware grounding. Our contributions are as follows: 1. Holistic Evaluation Framework. OmniCompass unifies target-guided omni-modal video grounding and understanding across four dimensions: paired Text and Text+Image specifications, VL/AV evidence tracks, TG/SG/QA tasks, and short-to-long videos. We introduce CS to jointly assess task correctness and consistency across paired target specifications. 2. Diverse, Rigorously Verified Benchmark. OmniCompass spans 820 videos, 80.6 hours, seven domains, Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 3 / 35 and 52 subcategories, with 240 videos shared between VL and AV tracks. Construction required about 1,800 human-hours for annotator training, calibration, annotation, expert adjudication, and revision. All instances undergo multi-round quality verification. 3. Diagnostic Evaluation of MLLMs. We evaluate 50 different MLLMs, revealing an overall advantage for proprietary models, especially in audio-visual understanding. Strong QA performance coexists with weak grounding and cross-specification inconsistency. Further analyses examine the effects of target specifications, video duration, timestamps, and input modalities.

2.2 Video Understanding Benchmarks
Table 1 compares existing benchmarks across four design dimensions. (i) Target Specification defines how the
target is presented. Most benchmarks use textual questions or instructions (Fu et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2026),
while IV-Bench (Ma et al., 2026) pairs text with a reference image for visual specification. (ii) Video Evidence
distinguishes visual and audio-visual requirements. Vision-language benchmarks assess appearance, motion, and
temporal relations. TempCompass (Liu et al., 2024b) evaluates temporal perception, while MotionBench (Hong
et al., 2025) targets fine-grained motion. WorldSense (Hong et al., 2026) and JointAVBench (Chao et al.,
2026) require synchronized visual and native-audio evidence. (iii) Task Coverage defines the expected output.
Question-answering benchmarks (Fu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026) produce semantic responses, while grounding
benchmarks require explicit evidence localization. OmniGround evaluates temporal intervals and spatial
regions (Gao et al., 2026), and V-STaR (Cheng et al., 2026) jointly assesses TG, SG, and QA. (iv) Video
Duration sets the temporal scope for evidence integration. MVBench emphasizes local actions and temporal
dynamics (Li et al., 2024b), whereas LongVideoBench (Wu et al., 2024), MLVU (Zhou et al., 2025a), and
LVBench (Wang et al., 2025a) stress long-context management across distant moments. LongVideoBench also
evaluates referring reasoning over interleaved video frames and subtitles. Existing benchmarks cover selected
dimensions or fixed combinations, limiting diagnosis of target identification, grounding, and omni-modal
reasoning across different target and evidence settings.
sections.content: OmniCompass unifies these dimensions through paired target-specification settings, complementary evidence tracks, and TG, SG, and QA across video durations. It supports diagnosis of target identification, spatio-temporal grounding, and event understanding under paired reference settings. Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 4 /

sections.title: 3 The OmniCompass Benchmark
sections.content: OmniCompass evaluates omni-modal video grounding and understanding along the dimensions in Table 1. Figure 2 summarizes the evaluation workflow. Each instance uses paired Text and Text+Image specifications of the same target. OmniCompass-VL evaluates vision-language models on visually resolvable tasks, while OmniCompass-AV evaluates omni-modal models using joint visual and native-audio evidence. Both tracks cover TG, SG, and QA across short (30s 𝑡 < 90s), medium (90s 𝑡 < 300s), and long (𝑡 300s) videos.

and a reference image
rimage jointly specify the target. For example, “When does the player complete the dunk?” requires the image

3.2 Benchmark Construction
Constructing OmniCompass requires approximately 1,800 human-hours for paired annotation, targeted revision,
and multi-round quality verification, following the pipeline in Figure 3.
Stage 1: Video Collection and Curation. We construct a pool of 8,489 candidate videos from nine public
datasets and supplement it with 240 self-collected videos from films, TV series, variety shows, and news
programs. The resulting pool covers seven high-level domains. Appendix Table C1 details the selection scope,
characteristics, usage terms, and contributions of the public datasets to the final benchmark.
sections.content: We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct to profile each public candidate with structured entity, action, attribute, and scene cues. Excluding videos shorter than 30 seconds or missing any of the four referential cue types leaves 6,946 eligible videos. We rank them by four predefined criteria: reference necessity, grounding suitability, temporal-spatial utility, and evidence diversity (Appendix Table C2). Shortlisting follows domain, duration, source, and subcategory constraints. Manual review retains 580 high-quality videos; with 240 self-collected videos, OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos. The same 240 videos form OmniCompass-AV, with additional audio-visual task annotations. Appendix details profiling, filtering, and scoring. Stage 2: Task Annotation and Construction. lead expert provides two days of task-specific training to four professional annotators before full-scale annotation. The team follows four principles to ensure consistent target specification and evidence across TG, SG, and QA under paired Text and Text+Image settings. (i) Same-Target Pairing. Each Text and Text+Image pair shares the same video, target, task semantics, and ground truth. In Text+Image, the textual expression requires the reference image to identify the target. (ii) Diverse Reference Types and Sources. References cover entity, action, attribute, and scene cues Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 5 / 35 Figure 3. Data construction pipeline. OmniCompass requires about 1,800 human-hours for rigorous annotation, verification, and revision. Stage 1: We screen 8,489 videos from nine public datasets, retain 6,946 after duration and referential-cue filtering, and select 580 to complement 240 self-collected videos. Stage 2: Four trained annotators independently construct paired Text and Text+Image TG, SG, and QA instances. AV cases include native audio. Stage 3: Annotators cross-verify and revise cases before final acceptance and correction by the lead expert, yielding 820 videos across seven domains, paired settings, two tracks, three tasks, and three duration groups. using video crops or semantically matched external images. Each image identifies the target without revealing the annotated event or answer evidence. For video-internal references, annotators favor separate view outside the target interval or QA clue interval whenever available. (iii) Precise TG/SG Labels. TG intervals tightly cover complete target-related events, while SG boxes localize the same target at both interval boundaries. (iv) Evidence-Grounded QA Design. Following CG-Bench (Chen et al., 2025a), annotators pair clue interval with five mutually exclusive options: one correct answer and four plausible distractors. The annotators first conduct pilot annotation on 30 VL and 30 AV videos spanning all seven domains and three duration types. Each video receives one TG, one SG, and one QA instance under paired Text and Text+Image settings, yielding 180 task instances. The pilot exposes inconsistencies in target pairing, temporal boundaries, spatial target consistency, and QA evidence. The lead expert reviews these cases with the team, resolves ambiguities, and refines the guidelines. The annotators then independently construct the remaining instances under the calibrated protocol. Guideline training, pilot calibration, and initial task construction across both tracks and all three tasks account for approximately 960 annotator-hours. Stage 3: Quality Verification and Finalization. All annotated cases undergo case-level quality verification before release. Four annotators independently cross-check annotations from their peers against the Stage 2 principles: same-target pairing, reference diversity and non-leakage, precise TG/SG labels, and evidencegrounded QA design. They inspect temporal-event completeness, boundary-frame box alignment, and the uniqueness and evidential support of QA answers. For AV cases, they also verify native-audio dependence and audio-visual alignment. They correct clear annotation errors, recheck the revised cases, and submit the confirmed cases to the lead expert. The expert resolves remaining inconsistencies, makes necessary corrections, performs final acceptance, and audits the release-ready data. These steps require approximately 320 annotator-hours and 500 lead-expert-hours. Appendix details the process. Tables D1 and D2 report video-level verification results and typical issues; Table D3 details human effort by stage and role.

4.1 Experimental Setting
Evaluated Models. We evaluate 50 models across tracks. OmniCompass-VL evaluates vision-language
models including proprietary models Gemini series (Google, 2025), GPT series (OpenAI, 2026a,b,c), Seed
series (Seed, 2026), and the Qwen close-source series (Qwen Team, 2026a). The open-source models cover
Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (Zeng et al., 2026a), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI,
2026), MiMo-V2.5 (MiMo-V2.5), the Qwen open-source series (Qwen Team, 2026b; Team, 2026a; Bai
et al., 2025), InternVL3.5-38B (Wang et al., 2025b), Keye-VL-2.0-30B-A3B (Team et al., 2026), TimeLens
series (Zhang et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026), and the LLaVA series (An et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2024).
OmniCompass-AV evaluates omni-modal models with native audio support, including the Gemini series,
Qwen-Omni series (Team, 2026b; Qwen Team, Alibaba, 2025), and Seed-2.0-Lite/Mini (Seed, 2026), as well
as MiMo-V2.5 (MiMo-V2.5), video-SALMONN 2+ (Tang et al., 2025), MiniCPM-o-4.5-8B (Cui et al., 2026),
Ola-7B (Liu et al., 2025), VideoLLaMA2-7B (Cheng et al., 2024), and VITA-1.5-7B (Fu et al., 2025b).
Implementation Details. (i) Frame sampling: We uniformly sample 64 frames for proprietary models and
open-source models with over 100B total parameters, and 32 for smaller models. GPT-series models use 49
frames to accommodate the Text+Image reference within the 50-image limit. VITA-1.5-7B follows its official
16-frame limit. Following TimeLens (Zhang et al., 2026), each frame is immediately preceded by its timestamp
in seconds. (ii) Input modalities: OmniCompass-VL excludes audio, while OmniCompass-AV adds the
native audio following WorldSense (Hong et al., 2026) and Video-MME-v2 (Fu et al., 2026). In Text+Image,
the reference image follows these inputs and immediately precedes the task prompt. Appendix E details the
experimental setup, input serialization, and task-specific prompts and response formats.

below 69.8% for Causal Reasoning. (ii) Visual References Benefit Proprietary Models and Grounding.
Text+Image improves average performance for 11 of the 36 models: 8 of 12 proprietary models and 3 of 24
open-source models. Among the open-source models with fewer than 100B parameters, only Qwen3.8-27B
improves. It gains 1.9% and 1.5% in TG mtIoU and SG msIoU but loses 2.2% in QA accuracy. Visual cues
may aid target matching while omitting useful textual detail. (iii) Larger Models Do Not Lead Every Task.
Within Qwen3.5, 397B exceeds 122B in CSAvg, 37.2% versus 33.5%, but trails in CSTG, 23.1% versus 24.3%.
Likewise, 27B trails 9B in CSSG, 15.3% versus 17.7%. (iv) Cross-Reference Consistency Remains Limited.
Across 36 models, CSTG, CSSG, and CSQA average 4.3%, 4.6%, and 6.4% below the lower corresponding
single-setting score. Strong single-setting results do not ensure correctness across settings.

(ii) Open-Source Models Lag Most in Audio-Visual Event Binding. In Figure 5(b), the best proprietary and open-source CSQA scores differ by 12.5% on Speech Understanding. The gap reaches 38.9% on Event Understanding, which requires linking audio cues to visible entities, actions, or scene context. (iii) Reference Effects and Consistency Gaps Persist with Audio. Text+Image improves SG msIoU and QA accuracy for 12 of 17 models each, but TG mtIoU for only five. MiMo-V2.5 achieves 59.2% and 58.7% QA accuracy under Text and Text+Image, respectively, but only 47.3% in CSQA. Similar aggregate accuracy therefore does not ensure correct answers on the same eligible pairs across settings. Figure 5. Fine-grained QA performance across tracks. We report category-wise CSQA scores in percent. Across both tracks, open-source models trail proprietary models, especially in audio-visual understanding. Cross-reference consistency, fine-grained perception, and audio-visual event binding remain challenging. Future models therefore need stronger multimodal alignment and audio-aware grounding.

On the VL track, Gemini-3.8-Flash, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, and Qwen3.8-27B gain 7.0%, 10.4%, and 2.3%, averaging 6.5%. On the AV track, Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash gain 3.6% and 6.2%, averaging 4.9%. VL gains concentrate in TG: Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B gain 18.3% and 18.2%. In AV, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash gains 16.0% in SG, while TG changes by -0.2% to +0.8% across both models. QA improves in every comparison by 0.7%5.9%. Text-only retains both question wordings but removes all media, including reference images. Its CSTG is only 0.10.8%, versus 18.8%30.1% in CSQA. Vision improves all 12 model-task comparisons. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we introduce OmniCompass, holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and It unifies TG, SG, and QA across VL and AV tracks with paired Text and Text+Image understanding. specifications for the same video, target, task semantics, and ground truth. The benchmark covers 820 manually annotated videos across seven domains, including 240-video AV subset with native audio. The paired settings and CS metric assess both prediction correctness and consistency under changes in target specification. Leading proprietary models outperform open-source models, especially in audio-visual understanding, while precise grounding, fine-grained perception, and audio-visual event binding remain challenging. Reference images yield task-dependent effects, while timestamps improve model performance in both tracks. These findings motivate stronger multimodal alignment and audio-aware grounding to connect target specifications with the relevant events and evidence. OmniCompass supports joint evaluation of QA, precise grounding, and cross-reference consistency across tasks and modalities, providing basis for diagnosing model limitations and measuring progress toward reliable omni-modal video understanding. sections.content: A.1 Performance across Video Durations Figure A1 compares ten models across short, medium, and long videos in OmniCompass-VL. All ten score lower on long than short videos in TG. Seed-2.1-Pro-260915 shows the largest decline, from 33.4% to 15.1%, while Gemini-3.8-Flash falls from 33.8% to 21.0%. Only five models decline in SG and six in QA. Thus, the direction of the duration association is more consistent for temporal localization than for the other tasks. These groups also differ in content and target granularity, so the comparison does not isolate video duration as the cause of lower scores. Figure A1. Performance across video durations in OmniCompass-VL. Bars show task-specific CS in percent for short videos below 90 seconds, medium videos from 90 to below 300 seconds, and long videos of at least 300 seconds. Each model uses its own eligible pairs. Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 16 / 35 A.2 Grounding across Target Granularity Figure A2 compares ten VL models and six AV models across relative target-duration and box-area groups. All ten VL models improve monotonically in TG as the relative target duration increases. All six AV models also peak in the highest duration-ratio quartile. Gemini-3.8-Flash rises from 7.9% to 43.1% on VL and from 27.1% to 56.2% on AV between the extreme groups. Spatial trends differ: every VL model peaks in the largest-box group, whereas every AV model peaks in the third quartile. Gemini-3.8-Flash scores 65.5% in the third AV quartile and 53.6% in the fourth. Quartile boundaries are computed from all videos separately for each track; scores use the common eligible pairs within each task. The resulting groups are not equal in size, and their boundaries differ between VL and AV. IoU also depends on target extent, so these curves describe associations rather than an isolated granularity effect. This contrast does not isolate audio effects: tasks, target distributions, and model rosters differ. Figure A2. Grounding across target granularity. Curves report CSTG and CSSG in percent across quartiles of target-to-video duration and mean endpoint box-to-frame area. Quartiles are track-specific; models share eligible pairs within each track and task. A.3 Performance across Video Domains Figure A3 compares the ten VL models across seven domains. All ten obtain their lowest SG and QA scores in Traffic, with equal-weight model means of 7.8% and 37.3%. Variety has the lowest mean TG score at 8.1%, but the highest mean SG score at 26.6%. Strong spatial grounding can therefore coexist with weak temporal localization within the same domain. These rankings apply to the shared eligible subsets, not necessarily every video in each domain. Domain comparisons also reflect differences in duration, target size, and QA content.

sections.content: B.1 Impact of Frame Scaling Increasing the frame budget improves performance in most settings, but the effect depends on the track and task. On OmniCompass-VL, all three tasks improve significantly for both models from 8 to 128 frames. TG CS increases by 22.2% and 19.6% for Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, respectively; SG increases by 22.8% and 16.9%, while QA increases by 20.0% and 18.6%. The gains are smaller and more task-dependent on OmniCompass-AV. SG improves by 18.3% for Gemini-3.8-Flash and 22.3% for Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, while QA improves by 9.9% and 13.4% from 8 to 128 frames. In contrast, TG remains nearly unchanged. We suppose that audio already provides useful temporal cues for AV TG (see Figure 7), leaving denser visual sampling with limited additional temporal evidence, whereas SG and QA can benefit from finer spatial details and richer visual context. Besides, more frames also increase visual input and inference cost, so the preferred budget depends on the task and track rather than always favoring the largest setting. C.2 Task-Oriented Candidate Scoring Candidate ranking combines reference necessity 𝑅, grounding suitability 𝐺, temporal-spatial utility 𝑇, and evidence diversity 𝐸 as 𝑆 = 0.35𝑅 + 0.25𝐺 + 0.25𝑇 + 0.15𝐸. These heuristic components use structured profiling statistics, not model evaluation scores. Table C2 defines the recorded component calculations on zero-to-ten scale. Scores inform shortlisting together with domain, duration, source, and subcategory coverage; human curation determines the retained public set. C.3 Question-Answering Taxonomy QA types are grouped by the dominant operation needed to answer each question. Perception covers direct recognition and judgments from the available evidence, while reasoning covers temporal, causal, or comparative relations. Both tracks use five answer options, but their type sets differ because AV questions are designed to draw on speech, sound, or joint audio-visual evidence. The shared format standardizes scoring without equating difficulty across tracks. OmniCompass-VL contains eight QA types, listed in Table C3 and shown in Figure C3. Fact Recognition, Action Recognition, Attribute Perception, Visual Counting, and Spatial Perception form the perception group. Event Understanding links audible cues to visible participants, actions, states, or context. These labels describe intended evidence requirements, rather than measured guarantee that every item fails when audio is removed. C.4 Reference Design and Provenance Reference images identify target through entity, action, attribute, or scene information, as defined in Table C5. The unit of analysis is task-specific reference, not unique image file or video. Each of the 820 VL videos contributes one reference for TG, SG, and QA, yielding 2,460 task instances. Tasks can select different targets; their cue types and sources are counted separately. Entity cues account for 1,960 of the 2,460 references, or 79.7%. The remaining references comprise 171 action cues, 200 attribute cues, and 129 scene cues. The examples include recognizable actions in Sports and appearance-based vehicle distinctions in Traffic. Figure C4 reports domain-wise frequencies; the cue types are not equally represented in this set. The reference set contains 1,933 video-internal images and 527 Internet images. Video-internal crops preserve the identity of targets specific to recording, while external exemplars can specify recognizable people, objects, or actions. Source selection follows the identification needs of each annotation rather than fixed per-domain quota. This variation is part of the benchmarks reference conditions and is not an independently controlled source-modality experiment. For video-internal references, annotation guidelines favor separate view outside the target interval or QA clue interval whenever one is available. Reviewers also inspect whether the image reveals the answer event, since temporal separation alone does not rule out semantic leakage. Crops retain target-identifying content while limiting irrelevant context and direct answer evidence. These checks aim to separate target specification from the evidence needed to solve the task.

sections.title: E Evaluation Protocols and Prompts
sections.content: E.1 Inputs and Paired Settings Frames are sampled uniformly across full videos. The standard budget is 64 for proprietary models and open-source models above 100B total parameters, and 32 otherwise.
